corrected_answer:
Scenario variant 83.

Assumptions (state these before touching anything): single-node or multi-rank LLM serving with a paged KV cache; the OOM is a device-side CUDA OOM, not host RAM exhaustion; prompts are long-context (>=8k tokens); the failure is load-dependent — it appears only after several concurrent requests, so a single request in isolation succeeds. If any of these is false the prioritization below changes and must be redone.

Primary falsifiable hypothesis.
H1: OOM is driven by aggregate KV-cache demand scaling with concurrency, not by any single long request. Formally: peak device bytes ~= weights + activation working set + sum_i(KV(len_i)); OOM occurs when concurrent admitted sequences push sum_i(KV) past the preallocated cache pool and the engine still tries to allocate transient activation buffers outside the pool.

How to falsify it.
H1 is FALSE if a single request at max_model_len succeeds repeatedly while the same total token count split across 8 concurrent requests also succeeds, i.e. failure does not track aggregate admitted tokens.

Controlled experiment.
Concurrency sweep: fix prompt length L=16k, output=256, sweep concurrency C in {1,2,4,6,8,12,16}, 3 repeats each, randomized order, 60s cooldown and a fresh engine process per arm. Record first-OOM concurrency C*. Primary metric: P(OOM) per arm; secondary: peak torch.cuda.max_memory_reserved and KV blocks in use.

Prioritized diagnosis order (cheapest and most diagnostic first): (1) read the engine's effective config and the computed worst-case KV footprint; (2) capture the allocator state at failure (allocated vs reserved, snapshot); (3) decompose device memory into weights / KV pool / residual across concurrency; (4) separate prefill steps from decode steps in the failure timeline; (5) check preemption and free-block counters; (6) confirm no co-tenant process shares the device.

Mitigations, in order of preference.
1) Admission control: cap max_num_seqs and max_num_batched_tokens so worst-case KV fits the pool with >=10% headroom. 2) Enable paged KV + prefix caching to cut duplicated prefix blocks. 3) Only then consider KV quantization (fp8) which trades accuracy and must be re-evaluated on task metrics.

Confounders to control: warm vs cold cache, CUDA graph capture on first steps, thermal/clock drift over long runs, background co-tenants, and client retry behaviour. Randomize arm order, restart the engine between arms, and replay an identical recorded request trace so arms are input-identical.

Rollback gates (pre-commit, must be written down before the change): revert if p95 TTFT regresses >15% vs the 7-day baseline, if p99 end-to-end latency regresses >20%, if throughput drops >10% at the target SLO, or if any OOM occurs in a 30-minute soak at 1.25x peak observed concurrency. Roll out canary -> 10% -> 50% -> 100% with at least 30 minutes at each step and automatic revert on gate breach.

What I would NOT do: raise gpu_memory_utilization to make the symptom disappear. That shrinks the non-KV headroom the engine needs for activations and comm buffers and converts a predictable admission-control failure into a rarer, harder-to-reproduce one under a slightly different traffic mix.

Scenario variant 91.

Assumptions (state these before touching anything): single-node or multi-rank LLM serving with a paged KV cache; the OOM is a device-side CUDA OOM, not host RAM exhaustion; prompts are long-context (>=8k tokens); the failure is load-dependent — it appears only after several concurrent requests, so a single request in isolation succeeds. Primary falsifiable hypothesis.
H8: the OOM is caused by prefix-cache or block-table growth that is never reclaimed — cached blocks from earlier long prompts are retained under an LRU that cannot evict fast enough when many new long prompts arrive together.

How to falsify it.
H8 is FALSE if free KV blocks are plentiful immediately before the failure, or if disabling prefix caching leaves the OOM rate unchanged.

Controlled experiment.
Track free/used KV blocks and cache hit rate at 1s resolution. Arms: A = prefix caching on, B = off, C = on with a reduced cache fraction. 5 repeats on the same replayed trace. Primary: OOM rate; secondary: TTFT p50 (prefix caching should improve it — quantify what you lose by disabling).

Prioritized diagnosis order (cheapest and most diagnostic first): (1) read the engine's effective config and the computed worst-case KV footprint; (2) capture the allocator state at failure (allocated vs reserved, snapshot); (3) decompose device memory into weights / KV pool / residual across concurrency; (4) separate prefill steps from decode steps in the failure timeline; (5) check preemption and free-block counters; (6) confirm no co-tenant process shares the device.

Mitigations, in order of preference.
1) Bound the reusable-block fraction so a floor of free blocks always exists. 2) Make eviction proactive at a watermark instead of on-demand at exhaustion. 3) Keep prefix caching if hit rate is high — disabling it is a diagnostic, not necessarily the fix.

Confounders to control: warm vs cold cache, CUDA graph capture on first steps, thermal/clock drift over long runs, background co-tenants, and client retry behaviour. Randomize arm order, restart the engine between arms, and replay an identical recorded request trace so arms are input-identical.

Rollback gates (pre-commit, must be written down before the change): revert if p95 TTFT regresses >15% vs the 7-day baseline, if p99 end-to-end latency regresses >20%, if throughput drops >10% at the target SLO, or if any OOM occurs in a 30-minute soak at 1.25x peak observed concurrency. Roll out canary -> 10% -> 50% -> 100% with at least 30 minutes at each step and automatic revert on gate breach.

What I would NOT do: raise gpu_memory_utilization to make the symptom disappear. That shrinks the non-KV headroom the engine needs for activations and comm buffers and converts a predictable admission-control failure into a rarer, harder-to-reproduce one under a slightly different traffic mix.
